title: Ukraine Strikes Iran-Linked Ship in Caspian, Oil Plunges on US-Iran Pause, Trump Dismisses Netanyahu on F-35s
subhead: Trump told reporters 'nobody tells me what we should be selling' when asked about Netanyahu's opposition to F-35 sales to Turkey, a day before the two leaders meet at the White House. Ukraine's long-range drone strike on an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea — killing one sailor — merged two wars that Turkey has been trying to keep separate. And oil fell below $91 as a weekend pause in US-Iran strikes opened a narrow diplomatic window.

sections.heading: Trump Brushes Off Netanyahu on F-35 Sale to Turkey
sections.body:
US President Donald Trump dismissed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's opposition to selling F-35 fighter jets to Turkey, telling reporters aboard Air Force One on July 27: 'Nobody tells me what we should be selling.' He added that Turkey has been 'a tremendous ally for me' and described it as 'a very powerful country' with a 'tremendous military,' according to Firstpost.

The comments came a day before Netanyahu was due at the White House, where the F-35 question is expected to feature prominently. Netanyahu had told Fox News earlier this month that Turkey is 'a regime infected by the Muslim Brotherhood' and that he does not think Ankara should receive F-35s or even engines for its fighter jets.

Trump's public rebuke of Netanyahu carries weight because it signals that the political will at the top favors the sale — but the statutory barriers remain. The State Department wrote to Congress last week confirming that Turkey has not yet met the conditions for F-35 delivery: it must no longer possess the S-400 system, provide assurances against future acquisition, and satisfy remaining certification requirements. Trump said during his July 7 Ankara visit that S-400 sanctions would be lifted, but the State Department letter confirmed they remain in place.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between Trump's personal enthusiasm and the legal requirements is the entire story. The presidential signal is clear, but Congress and the State Department have not moved. Turkey's path to the F-35 still runs through the S-400 resolution — and Trump's dismissal of Netanyahu doesn't change the statutory conditions.

sections.heading: Ukraine Strikes Iranian Vessel in Caspian Sea, Killing One Sailor
sections.body:
Ukraine carried out a long-range drone strike on an Iranian-linked cargo vessel in the Caspian Sea on July 25, killing one sailor and wounding another, according to Iran's Foreign Ministry. Iran confirmed the fatality and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned that the attack 'cannot go unanswered,' calling it an act of aggression, MSN and Iran's official news agencies reported.

The strike targeted a vessel that Ukrainian and Western intelligence sources say was part of an Iran-Russia military supply chain, transporting drones and ammunition across the Caspian to Russian ports. Ukraine dismissed Iran's threats, with officials in Kyiv framing the operation as a legitimate strike on a military logistics route. The Guardian reported that President Zelenskyy has also accused Iran of providing Russia with satellite imagery for directing strikes.

The attack opens a new geographic front linking the Ukraine and Iran conflicts. The Caspian Sea — bordered by Russia, Iran, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and Azerbaijan — had until now been a relative backwater in both wars. For Turkey, the convergence is significant: Ankara has been working to maintain separate channels with Moscow, Kyiv, and Tehran, and the Caspian strike complicates that balancing act by turning a shared waterway into an active military theater.
sections.whyItMatters: Two conflicts Turkey has tried to compartmentalize are now physically overlapping in the Caspian. Turkey shares the Black Sea with Russia and Ukraine and maintains economic ties with Iran — any escalation in the Caspian directly affects a corridor Turkey depends on for energy and trade transit.

sections.heading: Oil Drops Below $91 as US-Iran Strike Pause Fuels De-escalation Hopes
sections.body:
Brent crude fell nearly 10% to below $91 per barrel on Monday after the United States and Iran paused military strikes over the weekend, with no attacks reported from either side since Friday, according to Reuters and France 24. The drop reversed some of the premium built up during two weeks of sustained US-Iran strikes and Hormuz disruption.

Trump said over the weekend he was giving 'space for diplomacy,' and mediators in Oman and Qatar reported progress on a potential ceasefire framework. Iran's Foreign Ministry said there are 'no talks underway with the US,' though the pause in strikes itself signals de-escalation. Germany's Foreign Minister Wadephul confirmed Berlin remains ready to contribute to a Hormuz mine-clearing mission, and the US pressed the UK to host a coalition summit on the operation next week, MSN reported.

But the pause is fragile. Saudi Arabia intercepted Iranian-backed militia drones targeting its oil facilities over the weekend, and the Houthis struck two Saudi tankers in the Red Sea earlier this month. The mine-clearing operation in Hormuz — involving over 80 Iranian-laid mines — is expected to take weeks even with autonomous drone systems, according to a Defense News report on the US-led coalition push. The Conversation reported that global shipping will not return to normal for months even if the strait reopens.
sections.whyItMatters: For Turkey, oil below $91 is meaningful relief for the current account and inflation outlook — the CBRT held at 37% last week partly because of energy-cost pressure. But the drop is a pause, not a reversal. Mine-clearing in Hormuz will take weeks, Red Sea attacks continue, and the underlying supply disruption persists until shipping routes genuinely normalize.

sections.heading: Iraq and Syria Sign Pipeline MoU to Route Oil via Mediterranean
sections.body:
Iraq's cabinet authorized the signing of a memorandum of understanding with Syria's Ministry of Energy to build a crude oil export pipeline linking Iraqi production sites to global markets via the Mediterranean, The National reported on July 26. The director general of Basra Oil Company was authorized to sign the agreement.

The pipeline would give Iraq a second direct export route to the Mediterranean, reducing its dependence on both the Strait of Hormuz — where Iran's disruptions have cut Iraqi exports from 4.2 million bpd in February to roughly 1.45 million bpd in May, according to OPEC data — and the existing Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline through Turkey, which has faced repeated political and technical disruptions.

The Iraqi cabinet also approved an MoU with a consortium of ConocoPhillips, TI Capital, and Novaterra to assess exploration and development at the Akkas gas field near the Syrian border — one of Iraq's largest undeveloped gas fields. The decisions followed Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's visit to Washington, where he secured $200 billion in energy-sector MOUs with US companies, according to Iraq's Oil Minister Bassim Khudair.

The cabinet statement did not specify the pipeline's capacity, timeline, or financing. The plan revives a dormant route: a Kirkuk-to-Baniyas pipeline operated before being shut down by war and sanctions.
sections.whyItMatters: Iraq is racing to build alternatives to Hormuz, and Turkey's Ceyhan corridor gains a potential competitor. If the Syria route becomes operational, Iraq could reduce its dependence on Turkish transit — but the timeline is uncertain, and the security conditions in Syria remain volatile. For now, Ceyhan remains Iraq's only functioning Mediterranean outlet.

sections.heading: Kazakhstan Halves Oil Output After Ukrainian Drone Strikes on Russian Terminal
sections.body:
Kazakhstan has more than halved its daily oil output after the closure of its main export terminal on Russia's Black Sea coast, which was knocked out by Ukrainian drone attacks, Reuters reported citing an industry source. Production at the Tengiz field — Kazakhstan's largest — fell to approximately 406,000 barrels per day on July 22, down from a July average of 925,000 bpd, according to MSN.

The Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal at Novorossiysk, which handles the bulk of Kazakh crude exports, suspended operations after Ukrainian drone strikes on the facility. Kazakhstan is among the world's 10 biggest oil producers and its crude flows through CPC to Novorossiysk, and then by tanker through the Turkish Straits to world markets.

For Turkey, the impact is indirect but real: reduced Kazakh volumes through the Bosporus and Dardanelles mean less transit fee revenue and reduced tanker traffic. More critically, Kazakhstan's buyers are demanding alternative supply routes at a time when Hormuz is closed — and Kazakh Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov said customers are urging maximum available volumes because of the Hormuz disruption, OilPrice reported.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine's war on Russian logistics is now colliding with global oil supply chains that run through Turkish waters. Every barrel of Kazakh crude that stops flowing through the Turkish Straits is lost revenue — and the Caspian Sea strike on the Iranian vessel shows that the Black Sea and Caspian corridors Turkey depends on are both becoming active military zones.

sections.heading: Ozel's New Party Registers With 91 MPs, CHP Collapses to 44 Seats
sections.body:
Ozgur Ozel formally registered the New Party (Yeni Parti) with Turkey's Interior Ministry on July 24, after he and 90 other lawmakers resigned from the CHP. The party immediately became the second-largest bloc in the 600-seat parliament with 91 seats, behind the AKP's 277, while the rump CHP fell to 44 seats — dropping below both the DEM Party (56) and the MHP (46), according to AP and Bianet.

The CHP's Cyprus branch also defected to the New Party, following 91 MPs and numerous mayors. Ozel chose July 24 — the anniversary of the Treaty of Lausanne — to formalize the split, saying: 'May it be for the good of our homeland, our nation, our party and all of us.' He walked with his team to the First Parliament building, where the Republic's foundation was declared in 1923.

The split traces to a May court ruling that annulled the CHP's 2023 leadership congress, removed Ozel as chairman, and reinstated 77-year-old Kemal Kilicdaroglu. Ozel's faction appealed to the Court of Cassation, but the case was not heard before the judicial recess that began July 20. Kilicdaroglu rejected calls for an extraordinary congress, saying the CHP had 'largely completed its purification.'

Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu remains imprisoned since March 2025 on corruption and espionage charges. The New Party reportedly will not initially seek transfers from CHP mayors to avoid destabilizing local administrations. MiddleEastEye noted that the split is both good and bad news for Erdogan: it fragments the opposition but also creates a more dynamic rival that could attract voters the old CHP could not.
sections.whyItMatters: The opposition is now formally split between a 91-seat New Party and a 44-seat rump CHP. Whether this fragments or revitalizes the anti-Erdogan vote depends on whether the two formations can coordinate ahead of 2028 — and on whether Imamoglu's legal situation changes. For now, the AKP faces a fragmented opposition in a 600-seat parliament where 277 seats gives Erdogan a working majority with the MHP.

bottomLine: Trump's dismissal of Netanyahu on F-35 sales — 'nobody tells me what we should be selling' — is the most significant signal yet that the White House wants the deal done, but the statutory S-400 conditions remain unchanged. The Caspian Sea strike by Ukraine on an Iranian supply vessel merges two wars Turkey has tried to keep in separate compartments, turning a shared waterway into an active military theater. Oil fell below $91 on the US-Iran pause, offering Turkey's inflation outlook some breathing room — but the underlying supply disruption from Hormuz mines and Red Sea attacks persists. Iraq signed an MoU with Syria for a Mediterranean pipeline that could eventually compete with Turkey's Ceyhan corridor, while Kazakhstan's oil output halved after Ukrainian drones hit the Novorossiysk terminal — another reminder that the Black Sea route Turkey depends on is now a war zone. At home, Ozel's New Party is registered and seated with 91 MPs, confirming the opposition's permanent split.
sources: Firstpost, AP, Bianet, Reuters, MSN, The National, France 24, The Guardian, MiddleEastEye, OilPrice, Oilprice.com, Hurriyet Daily News, InvestingCube, The Conversation, Cleveland Jewish News, Jang News, MSN World
